beats.lead: A tool now used to edit human genes was first found by cheese and yoghurt scientists.
beats.text: In 2005, researchers at the food company Danisco were trying to work out why some batches of their bacterial starter cultures kept surviving virus attacks that should have wiped them out.
beats.note: The bacterium was Streptococcus thermophilus, used to make yoghurt and cheese.

beats.name: Rodolphe Barrangou and Philippe Horvath
beats.role: at Danisco, found that the surviving bacteria had copied new DNA sequences from the attacking viruses into a repeating region of their genome called CRISPR, making them immune to that exact virus next time.

beats.text: It took two more years to prove what this actually was: an adaptive immune system, one that lets bacteria remember viruses they have already survived.
beats.note: The proof was published in Science in March 2007, the first experimental evidence that CRISPR worked this way.

beats.text: The dairy industry's problem became biotechnology's tool five years later, when Jennifer Doudna and Emmanuelle Charpentier worked out how to combine CRISPR's two separate guide molecules into one.
beats.note: That single change, in 2012, turned a bacterial defence system into something that could be aimed at almost any piece of DNA.

beats.text: Charpentier and Doudna won the 2020 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for it. The bacteria that made it possible were just trying to survive being attacked by viruses in a yoghurt vat.

beats.line: Gene editing's origin story starts in a dairy factory.
